newsitem.title: UK: Non-OPEC 2Q oil output steady at 39.5 million bpd.
newsitem.headline: Non-OPEC 2Q oil output steady at 39.5 million bpd.

text.p: Oil output from the world's main non-OPEC suppliers steadied in second quarter 1997 as strong Asian growth was countered by slower production rates in North America and Europe, a Reuters survey found.
Output totalled 39.54 million barrels per day (bpd), a slender increase of just over 60,000 bpd on the first quarter.

The survey covers more than 90 percent of the oil pumped by suppliers other than the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and includes natural gas liquids, as well as crude, from most countries.
Asian producers made the strongest gains in the second quarter, boosting output by nearly three percent or 158,000 bpd with Australia, China and India the star performers.
Australian production jumped by around 80,000 bpd to 685,000 bpd thanks to the start up of the Wandoo field and gains at other fields in offshore Western Australia.
In China continued growth in offshore production helped add 30,000 bpd to the country's output tally, while India pumped an extra 33,000 bpd.
Output in Latin American non-OPEC countries increased by almost three percent, squeezing out an additional 83,000 bpd. Gains from Argentina and Brazil's offshore Campos Basin made key contributions.
But a slide in production rates in the United States, Canada and Britain was sharp enough to knock out gains elsewhere, the survey found.
Britain was the biggest loser. North Sea field maintenance and unexpected technical hitches combined to pull output down a hefty 289,000 bpd to 2.34 million bpd.
The fall cancelled out a large production increase in Norway of 203,000 bpd, while elsewhere in Europe output rates were mostly flat.
North American production dropped by 168,000 bpd, with U.S. output sliding 70,000 bpd to 8.209 million bpd, while Canada lost 115,000 bpd partly thanks to a fall in synthetic crude output.
Non-OPEC Middle East and African production was mostly steady in the second quarter. Angola and Yemen boosted production by around 20,000 bpd, but Egypt and Oman posted small losses.
Former Soviet states proved that they had turned the corner after years of sliding output rates.
Russian production steadied at 5.88 million bpd, while Kazakhstan added nearly 30,000 bpd and Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan also made small gains.
Figures in millions of barrels per day come mostly from national governments. Other sources include oil companies and the Paris-based International Energy Agency (IEA):
